I want to talk about the way light behaves in the late afternoon, because that is the thing that has stayed with me longest and because it is a good excuse to sit down and write 2500 words about nothing in particular. The sun is lower then, and it stops trying to be impressive. It is not blinding you anymore. It is horizontal, tired in a kind of generous way, and it slides across surfaces the way a hand might rest on a table.

It gets into the cracks of the city. It finds the brick between buildings that you never look at directly, and it makes that brick glow as if it had been waiting. The air is thicker. It smells like heat leaving. On days when it has rained in the morning, the asphalt still holds a faint steam, and the light catches it and turns the street into something briefly, impossibly clean.

I was thinking about this because I was asked to write. Not about anything specific. Just to write. For 2500 words. That is a strange request, and a kind one. It is permission to wander.

I live in a house with a kitchen window that faces west. In the summer the light comes in around four o'clock and it makes a rectangle on the floor. The rectangle moves. If I stand still in it, I am warm. If I move out of it, I am cool again. My cat knows this. She will arrange herself in the rectangle and then, when the rectangle moves off her, she will sigh and relocate, always with the same mild reproach, as if I had done something to the sun.

Children understand this better than adults. They will chase the patch of light across a room, or lie down in it and stare up at the ceiling, or try to trap it in a jar. I used to think it was a kind of magic, and I still do. There is no better proof that the world is made of attention. Light is only light. The room is only a room. But when they meet, something else happens.

Writing is similar. You put words down and you wait to see what happens where they meet the day. Sometimes nothing. Sometimes a rectangle of warmth appears and you sit in it for a while.

I have been reading a lot about memory lately, not in books so much as in the way my own memory keeps returning to the same few scenes and repainting them. The memory of my grandfather’s workshop, for instance. It was a small shed behind his house, with a single bulb hanging from the ceiling and a bench covered in oil. The light in there was always yellow and always a little dusty. He would work on small engines, taking them apart until they were a collection of shiny parts laid out in order, like a puzzle. He never lost a part. He had a way of knowing where everything belonged.

I remember the smell of metal and cutting oil and the faint sound of the radio playing in the next room. I remember sitting on a stool that was too tall for me and watching his hands move. They were big hands, scarred, with grease under the nails that never really came out. He would talk to me while he worked, not directly, but in a low voice, as if he were talking to the engine. “You have to listen,” he said once. “They tell you what they need if you’re patient.”

I didn’t understand then. I understand it now in a different way. Writing is like that. You have to listen to the sentence. You have to be patient with it. You can’t force it to work. You can try to, and you’ll get something, but it will be tight and it will hurt.

My grandfather died when I was seventeen. The workshop was cleared out. I took a small wooden mallet he had made from a piece of oak and a worn screwdriver with a black handle. The rest went to someone else. I sometimes wonder if the shed is still there. I think it probably isn’t. The house was sold. The new owners likely needed the space for a garden. It is a reasonable thought.

But I still have the memory of the light in there, and the way it made the metal parts look like they were alive. That memory is not accurate. I know it isn’t. Memory never is. It is a reconstruction. It is a story we tell ourselves about a story we told ourselves earlier. The light was probably not that good. The workshop was probably cold in the winter and stifling in the summer. But the memory has become a place I can go back to when I need to be quiet.

That is one of the things I love about language. It lets you build rooms you can return to. You can furnish them with whatever you need. You can leave the windows open or closed.

There is a park near where I used to live. It had a big oak tree in the middle of it, and a bench underneath it that faced away from the playground. People would sit there with coffee and newspapers. In the fall the leaves would fall and pile up around the bench, and no one would clean them up for weeks. The oak would drop acorns with a soft thud. Sometimes a squirrel would run up and down the trunk, and you could watch it for a long time without getting bored.

I would go there after school. I would do my homework on that bench. I would watch the light move across the grass. I remember one afternoon in particular because it rained lightly and then stopped, and the sun came out and everything smelled like wet earth. A woman walked her dog, and the dog stopped to sniff at the base of the oak, and the woman laughed and said, “He’s writing a novel about the tree.” I laughed too, but I thought about it later. It is a nice idea, that animals are writing novels about us, in their own way.

The park is gone now. They built apartments there. I walk past sometimes and I can still see the oak in my mind, and I can still feel the bench under me. The apartments are nice, I suppose. People need places to live. But the oak is not there. I have photos, but photos are not the same. Photos are proof, not presence.

We spend so much of our lives trying to hold onto presence. We take pictures, we write notes, we keep objects. The mallet, the screwdriver. The rectangle of light on the floor. We think if we can just capture it, we won’t lose it.

But we always lose it. That is the nature of things. The light moves. The seasons change. The people we love get older and then they are gone. You can’t stop it. You can only notice it as it happens. That is the work.

I think about the people who have lived in the houses I have lived in. Before me and after me. The walls have heard other voices. The kitchen has seen other hands. There is a particular kind of humility in that. You are a temporary resident. You are a caretaker for a while.

When I move out, someone else will sit at the table I sit at. They will look out the same window. The light will come in at four o’clock and make the same rectangle on the floor. They will have their own cat, or they won’t. They will have their own memories. The house will accumulate them, layer by layer, like varnish.

This is why I like old houses. You can feel the layers. The paint that has been painted over. The floorboards that have been worn down in certain spots. The way a door sticks in the summer and swings freely in the winter. It is a record of use. It is a kind of writing.

We are all writing, constantly, with our bodies, with our choices, with the small things we leave behind. A coffee ring on a table. A scratch on a windowsill. A plant that was loved and then forgotten.

I have a plant. It is a pothos. It grows slowly, and it is very forgiving. I forget to water it for weeks and it just droops a little and then perks up again when I remember. It is a good teacher. It doesn’t demand attention, it just asks for consistency. I like that.

In the late afternoon, the light comes through the kitchen window and hits the pothos, and the leaves turn a kind of translucent green. You can see the veins. It is beautiful in a quiet way. It doesn’t need to be beautiful. It just is.

I think about how many people have sat in the late afternoon light and felt something shift inside them, something softening. It is not a revelation, usually. It is not a lightning bolt. It is a small loosening. A remembering.

Sometimes I think the world is too loud. The notifications, the alerts, the endless scroll. It is hard to hear yourself think. But the late afternoon light is quiet. It doesn’t ask anything of you. It just arrives.

If I could give anyone one piece of advice, it would be to sit in that light for five minutes a day and do nothing. Don’t read, don’t scroll, don’t make a to-do list. Just sit. Feel the warmth on your skin. Watch the dust move in the air. Listen to the house settle.

It sounds simple, and it is. That is the trick of it. The simple things are the hardest to remember to do.

I have a friend who keeps a notebook by her bed. She writes one sentence a day. Not a journal, not a diary. Just one sentence. Sometimes it is, “The rain sounded like paper.” Sometimes it is, “I missed my mother today.” Sometimes it is, “I am tired.” She says it helps her feel like she is still here, like she is still paying attention.

I started doing that a few months ago. My notebook is messy. The handwriting gets worse as the night goes on. Some days I write a full page. Some days I write nothing. It doesn’t matter. The point is the return. The point is the habit of noticing.

Writing 2500 words on demand is not a habit, it is a sprint. But it is also a kind of noticing. You have to keep going, you have to keep finding the next sentence. You have to stay with it.

Sometimes the sentences come easily. Sometimes they feel like dragging a boulder. Both are fine. Both are part of it.

I wonder what the person who asked for this will do with it. Maybe they will read it all the way through. Maybe they will skim. Maybe they will never read it at all. That is okay too. The writing is its own event. It exists whether or not it is witnessed.

I think about the idea of freedom in writing. Free writing is not the same as careless writing. It is still work. It requires attention. You have to be free enough to follow a thought without judging it, but disciplined enough to keep going when the thought runs out.

That is what I am trying to do here. I am trying to stay with the day. I am trying to stay with the light.

The kettle is whistling in the kitchen. I should probably get up and make tea. But I want to stay here a little longer, in this rectangle of light, with these words.

If you are reading this, thank you for being here with me. I don’t know you, but you are sharing this space for a moment. That is enough.

I will end with an image. It is of a small boat on a lake at dusk. The water is glassy. The sky is pink and blue. The boat is still. No one is in it. It is just there, floating, being held up by the water. That is how I want to feel at the end of a day of writing. Held up. Still. Ready to float.

And the light will come again tomorrow, at four o’clock, and it will make another rectangle on the floor. And I will sit in it, if I remember to.
